input.question: Why do cars travel in packs on the highway, even when there are no traffic stops to create groups?
input.ground_truth: Faster cars inevitably stack up behind slow cars, generating this pack formation. Eventually the faster cars will weave through and "escape" until they hit the next pack, but there's always another slow-car-slowly-passing-even-slower-car up ahead to cause another group. The cars in a group do not stay together long, it's a transient phenomenon that forms and dissolves when cars with different speeds meet.

Okay! Imagine you and your friends are walking to school. If you all walk together, it feels safer and you can talk and laugh. Sometimes, cars do something similar on the highway.

Cars travel in packs or lines because it helps them be safe and save a little bit of gas. When one car moves, the cars behind it can follow easily without having to work as hard. It's like when you ride your bike and someone pushes you from behind—you go a little faster and easier!

Also, if cars stay close together, it helps them see each other better, so they know when to slow down or speed up. It's like playing follow the leader with your friends.

So, even when there’s no traffic stop, cars like to travel together because it feels safer and is a little easier for them!
